fields.meaning: Should be, ought to be | Surely ~
fields.connection: V・Aい plain form + はずだ / Na + な / N + の
examples: Today should be a holiday.
He should have arrived at the station by now.
The passport should be in this drawer.
Students wouldn't go to such an expensive place.
He was supposed to come, but he didn't.
There's no way that was his mistake.
fields.explain:
The basis for the inference needs to be clear (a timetable, what someone said, experience).
More refined when speaking politely: ～はずです／～はずでしょう（softer）.
Expresses a contradiction: ～はずなのに + a result contrary to expectation.
Strong negation: ～はずがない ＞ ～ないはずだ in terms of negative nuance.
Avoid using it for requests/commands; it is a judgment, not volition.

- Meaning: “Surely/by rights… (according to common sense, a plan, or a reason)”. The degree of conviction is higher than だろう/でしょう, based on clear grounds (information, a schedule, logic).
- Nuance: An assertion with grounds. In the negative ～はずがない, it is a strong negation because it goes against common sense/the grounds.
- Tense: ～はずだった expresses “should have/was planned”, often used with が／のに to state a contrary result.
- Combinations: Can be used with ある/いる/可能・受身・使役, etc.
fields.notes:
• N + の + はずだ is the standard form; avoid N + はずだ (without の) in formal written language.
• “来るはずだった” expresses an expectation at a point in time in the past; “来たはずだ” is a conjecture that something has surely happened.
• ～はずがない emphasizes negation based on common sense/what is known; it is stronger than ～ないはずだ.
• In polite speech: ～のはずです/～のはずではありません are used at work and in emails.
mistakes: Wrong linking particle with nouns: use Nのはずだ, not Nはずだ.
Confusing it with だろう/でしょう: when the question requires “firm grounds” → choose ～はずだ.
Confusing the past: 来るはずだった（expectation in the past）≠ 来たはずだ（conjecture that it happened）.
Combining it with a command/request is unnatural: × 来るはずだ、来なさい。

rows: Strong, based on intuition/evidence; close to はずだ but with a more subjective, assertive nuance
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>犯人<rt>はんにん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>いない。
Moral norms/rules, not a logical prediction
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>るべきだ。
Strong negation, more colloquial than ～はずがない
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けるわけがない。

fields.name: ～は～に　（causative-passive form）
fields.meaning: An expression combining the causative and the passive. Indicates having to do something because someone forced you to, or an emotion arising from some trigger.
fields.connection: N1は + N2に + V causative-passive form
examples: I was made to pay the cleaning fee.
When I was a child, my older brother often made me cry.
In high school, I was made to run as much as 10 km every day.
I'm always kept waiting by her.

fields.connection: N1は + N2ほど + A negative (～くありません/～ない)
examples: I'm not as tall as my older brother.
Japanese isn't as hard to pronounce as English.
It doesn't snow as much this year as it did last year.
This problem isn't as complicated as I thought.
He doesn't drink as much coffee as I do.
fields.explain:
Polite form/written language: ～くありません／～ではありません; spoken language: ～くない／～じゃない.
You can add それほど/思ったほど to adjust the standard of comparison: “not to that degree/not as much as I thought”.
The word order is fixed: AはBほど…ない. Do not move B into the subject position.

• “A is not as … as B” (comparison of inferiority in the negative form).
• ほど expresses “to the degree of B”; add ない/ありません to negate the degree of A compared with B.
• Used naturally for both qualities (tall, difficult) and actions (eat, study, speak).
fields.notes:
• With Aな/N: use ではない/ではありません, not ～くない.
• The subjective evaluation expressions “思ったほど～ない/予想したほど～ない” are very natural in essays.
• A can be omitted when the context is clear: 思ったほど難しくない。
mistakes: Wrong な-form: “親切くない” → correct: “親切ではない”.
Confusing the order: “BはAほど…” is not equivalent; A must stay as the item that is less.
Confusing it with より: AはBより～ is used when A is more than B, not as the negative form of inferiority.
Dropping ほど: “AはBない” is incorrect; ほど is the core of the comparison.

rows: A is not as … as B
Negative form of the comparison of inferiority
<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>ほど<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>くない
States the greater side, not used in the negative
<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>のほうが<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>い
～ほどではない／ほどでもない
Compares the degree with an abstract standard
<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>するほどではない
More casual, with a nuance of approximation
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>と<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じくらい<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い

fields.name: ～ば（conditional form）
fields.connection: Vば / Aければ / N・Naなら(ば) + [sentence/clause]
examples: If you leave home at 8:00, you'll probably make the 8:15 train.
"Can you read Japanese newspapers?" "Yes, if I use a dictionary."
If the weather is good, you can see Mt. Fuji from here.
"If you don't want to eat it, you don't have to."
"If you're free this Sunday, please come over."
If your Japanese isn't good, you can't do this job.
fields.notes:
Note:
●文末は過去形にならない。（＝結果が出ている文には使えない）
The end of the sentence cannot be in the past.(=cannot be used in a sentence where the result has already appeared)
X　クーラーをつけらば、すぐに涼しくなった。
X if I turn on the air conditioner, it immediately became cool
〇クーラーをつければ、すぐに涼しくなるだろう。
〇 If you turn on the air conditioner, it will probably get cool right away.
〇クーラーをつけたら、すぐに涼しくなった。
〇 when I turned on the air conditioner, it quickly became cool.

fields.name: ～ます in polite speech
fields.meaning: Polite form within compound sentences: ～まして/～ますので/～ますのに
examples: Hans ran a fever last night, and it still hasn't gone down this morning.
I'm keeping my child home from school today, so please pass that on to the teacher.
fields.explain: In spoken language, verbs are sometimes used like this: V ます まして、Vますので、Vますのに… to make speech sound more formal and polite.

fields.meaning: A sentence pattern expressing a time limit. ～まで is usually followed by sentences expressing a continuous action or state. へまでに is usually followed by sentences expressing a momentary action.
fields.connection: N/Vる + まで + [continuing action] / N/Vる + までに + [action at a point in time]
examples: I'll be waiting here until the plane's departure time.
Please don't go home until this work is finished.
I'll pay for the trip by the 20th.
Tidy up the room by the time the guests arrive, okay?

fields.meaning: It seems…, apparently… | It looks like ~
fields.connection: V・Aい plain form + ようだ / Na + な / N + の
examples: The light in the room is on. Ali seems to be in the room.
Tanaka seems to like singing. They're often singing.
"Please look at this map. It seems the station isn't very far from here."
"Whose notebook is this?" "It seems to be Tei's notebook, because it says T here."
My throat hurts. I seem to have caught a cold.
"Ou, you seem to have lost weight lately. What happened?"
fields.explain:
“～ようだ” is neutral and can be used in written language. Polite: ～ようです.
Comparison with “～みたいだ”: みたいだ is casual and colloquial; ようだ is more formal.
Use “～のように/～のような” when you want to turn it into an adverbial/attributive modifier.
When the degree of certainty is low or to soften the sentence, you can use: ～ようだと思う, ～ように感じる.
To describe a clearly visible appearance, そうだ（様態） is more natural:雨が降り そうだ (it looks like it's going to rain).

• Conjecture based on sensory/indirect evidence: “it seems/apparently”. Example: 声からすると彼のようだ。
• Metaphor/comparison: “like”. Example: 綿のように柔らかい。
• Describes outward appearance/a general impression, more objective than みたいだ in written language/for JLPT scoring.
• The form ～ように also indicates a goal/manner (a different meaning from conjecture): 間違えないように書く。
fields.notes:
• “かのようだ” strengthens the metaphorical nuance, written language: 何も知らないかのようだ。
• “～ようでは/ようじゃ” states a condition leading to a negative evaluation: そんなに勉強しないようでは合格できない。
• “～ようなら/ようだったら” is a hypothetical condition based on a judgment: 雨のようなら中止します。
• Watch the connection: Nのようだ, Aなようだ (not Nだようだ / Aだようだ).
mistakes: Wrong connection: 学生だようだ × → 学生のようだ 〇.
Confusing it with そうだ（様態）: “looks like it's going to rain” → 降りそうだ, not 降るようだ.
Overusing みたいだ in JLPT style: prefer ようだ/ようです in standard answers.
Forgetting to switch to Aな/ Nの when used as an attributive modifier: 夢のような vs 夢ような ×.

rows: <ruby>日本人<rt>にほんじん</rt></ruby>らしい<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>。
A source of information, not personal conjecture

fields.meaning: A way of quoting a command, advice, or a request.
examples: I was told to think about it.
My teacher told me not to forget my homework.
I was told to come 30 minutes earlier than usual tomorrow.
The person next to me told me to be a little quieter.

fields.name: ～ように（wish）
fields.meaning: Expresses a wish that something will become ~. Often used with verbs that do not include the speaker's volition (non-volitional verbs, verbs with a potential meaning (①）or verbs whose subject is a third person (②), etc.).
fields.connection: Vるように / Vないように + [sentence/clause]
examples: Let's sit toward the front so that we can hear the talk well.
I opened the window wide to let a nice breeze in.
On the snowy day, I left home early so that I wouldn't be late for school.
Be careful not to get hurt, okay?

fields.connection: V plain form + らしい らしく らしくない / N / Na / Aい
examples: I heard that Oyama is raising a cat he found. That's just like him, being such an animal lover.
"The color of that sweater is so springlike and lovely."
"You've got a job now, so act more like a working adult."
She's very healthy and has never had what you'd call a real illness.
Apparently he isn't coming.
I hear it's going to get cold tomorrow.
fields.explain:
Hearsay “らしい” expresses a conjecture based on a source (a rumor/what someone said); the speaker does not assert it with certainty.
“～そうだ” (hearsay) has the nuance of directly reporting what someone else said; “らしい” is indirect and softer, showing that the speaker is piecing together sources.
In the meaning “typical of”, “～らしい” is an i-adjective and can be conjugated as らしく, らしさ.

• Meaning 1 (hearsay): Based on information heard/an indirect source → “it seems/I heard that …”. A moderate degree of certainty, a conjecture from a source.
• Meaning 2 (typicality): Expresses being “truly/befitting” a noun according to a model/social characteristics.
• N/Na before らしい: do not use だ. Example: 便利らしい（do not say 便利だらしい）.
fields.notes:
1) It is easy to confuse ～らしい (befitting/typical) with ～らしい (I heard).
→ Here ～らしい expresses “full of the character of, true to the characteristics of N”.
2) It is not used to pass on rumors.
→ Rumors/hearsay usually use: 普通形＋らしい.
3) Often used with nouns of role, personality, or style.
→ The meaning is close to “suitable for, worthy of” (にふさわしい).
mistakes: Adding “だ” before らしい: ×便利だらしい → ○便利らしい。
Confusing “らしい” (hearsay) with “そうだ（様態）” meaning “looks like”: 雨が降りそうだ ≠ 雨が降るらしい.
Confusing “子どもらしい”（truly childlike, positive) with “子どもっぽい”（childish, can have a critical nuance).

rows: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>によると、<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みだそうだ。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>るようだ／みたいだ。
Colloquial, sometimes with a critical nuance
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもっぽい<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>。

examples: When I'm busy with work, I sometimes don't eat lunch.
This road sometimes freezes over in winter.
Foreigners sometimes can't read this kanji.
Some people don't like raw fish.
Trains are occasionally late.
Sometimes I'm so tired that I can't sleep.
fields.explain:
Often used with:時々, ときどき, たまに, まれに, よく (less often),人によっては,場合によっては.
In descriptions/rules: ～では…ことがある states a general possibility.
The negative “ないことがある” is softer than “ない”: “there are times when … not”.
Formal: ～ことがあります (~ます) keeps it polite in reports/presentations.

• An action/event happens “at times/sometimes” (not regularly, depending on the situation).
• Used to state a general possibility of occurrence, without committing to a specific frequency.
• A polite expression that reduces absoluteness; suitable when you want to soften a statement.
• The negative ないことがある states exceptions: “there are also times when … not”.
fields.notes:
• If you add も: V-ることもある → “there are also times when”, emphasizing one possibility among many.
• In technical documents/customer service, “～ことがあります” is used to avoid legal risk (no absolute commitment).
• Put “ごくまれに/稀に” in front to lower the probability: ごくまれにエラーが発生することがある。
mistakes: Confusing it with V-たことがある (experience): “日本へ行くことがある” ≠ “行ったことがある”.
Using the absolute simple present instead of the softening pattern: “必ず遅れる” → use “遅れることがある” when you are not sure.
Adding the wrong subject: “人は～ことがある” is too general; use a specific setting: この地域では～ことがある。

rows: A phenomenon that recurs under certain conditions
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れることがある
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったことがある
Somewhat stiff/more objective, used in instructions
<ruby>認証<rt>にんしょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>する<ruby>場合<rt>ばあい</rt></ruby>がある
<ruby>週末<rt>しゅうまつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>たりする

examples: Starting this year, I'll study English every day.
I decided not to drink for the sake of my health.
To save money, I make it a rule to eat out only once a week.
It's raining hard, so I'll go by car today.
Let's just say this never happened.
fields.explain:
First person in the present/past tense: emphasizes personal volition. With a third person, context is needed to show their intention.
～ことにしている expresses a habit and can be used with frequency words:毎日/いつも/なるべく.
In conversation, ～ことにする can carry the nuance of “having just decided”: よし、これにする！
Often appears with a reason: ～ので/ために + ことにする.

• Expresses a deliberate decision by the speaker/agent after consideration.
• ～ことにしている: the decision has turned into a personal habit/rule, still maintained by oneself.
• ～ということにする: to treat as…, used for a “temporary agreement/assumption”.
• An active nuance, in contrast to ～ことになる (a decision made by outside parties/a process).
fields.notes:
• In group plans, using ～ことにする sounds like you decided on your own; more polite: ～ことにしませんか (shall we decide on it together?).
• Nuance of timing: ことにした (already decided) vs ことにする (deciding right now/about to decide).
• When reporting someone else's volition, add ようだ/という: 彼は留学することにしたようだ。
mistakes: Confusing it with ことになる: “会社が決めた” → you must use ことになる, not ことにする.
Using ことにしている for a fresh decision: when you have just decided, ことにした is more natural.
Third person without grounds for their intention: 彼は来ることにした (needs context/a source of information).
Confusing it with ようにする: ようにする emphasizes effort, not a firm decision.

rows: It has been decided/end up having to
A decision made by outside parties/a process
<ruby>転勤<rt>てんきん</rt></ruby>することになった
Emphasizes effort, not necessarily a firm decision
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>るようにする
A nuance of “consider it as” rather than deciding to do
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>したということにする

fields.meaning: Means doing something before the action in the first clause is carried out.
fields.connection: Vる + とき（the action in the second clause happens first）
examples: When going
We say 「いただきます」 when we eat a meal.
I'll call you tomorrow when I leave the house.
Yesterday, when I went to bed, I set my alarm clock.
fields.notes: Takes the dictionary form of a verb expressing an action and indicates that another act or event takes place before that action is performed, or simultaneously in parallel with it. ① and ② are examples of the former, ③ and ④ of the latter.

fields.connection: Vる + ときに（not yet happened） / Vた + ときに（already happened）
examples: I bought a camera before I went to Japan.
I bought a camera when I was in Japan.
Please turn off the lights when you go out.
When I was a child, I often played in the river.
The busier you are, the more important it is to take breaks.
When you're in trouble, please feel free to talk to us.
fields.explain:
Used to set a time reference for the main action; the “とき(に)” clause can come either before or after.
With verbs of motion such as行く/来る/帰る: V-るとき usually = “before going/coming/returning”, V-たとき = “after having gone/come/returned”.
“に” is usually used when the main action happens exactly at that reference (a point in time); “に” is omitted when speaking in general (habits, situations).
Do not use “とき” for a strong cause-and-result relationship (use ～ので/から instead) or for conditions (see ～たら/～と).

• Expresses “when/at the time …” – a point in time at which another action/event takes place.
• V-るとき(に): the time reference is before or just before the action happens (for movement/going somewhere, it is usually understood as “before”).
• V-たとき(に): the time reference is after the action has taken place.
• “に” makes the “point” nature of the time clear; without “に” the meaning does not change much and has a more general nuance.
• The tense in the “とき” clause is relative tense, determining the before/after relationship with the main clause.
fields.notes:
• The tense in the “とき” clause is relative: 現在形 does not only mean “present” but “simultaneous/before” depending on the verb.
• With adjectives/nouns: Aい/ Aな/ Nの + とき expresses a state as a time reference.
• “ときどき” is an adverb meaning “sometimes”, not the structure “とき + とき”.
mistakes: Confusing V-るとき with V-たとき: 日本へ行くとき/行ったとき mean before going/after arriving.
Forgetting “の” with nouns: ×子どもとき → ○子どものとき.
Using “とき” instead of “あいだ” with an ongoing action: ×勉強するときずっと → ○勉強しているあいだずっと.
Overusing “に”: not grammatically wrong, but it can make the style heavy; choose according to nuance.
JLPT: trick questions often change the tense in the “とき” clause to test your understanding of the before/after relationship.

rows: A point in time; the tense in the subordinate clause determines before/after
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くとき/<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>ったとき
About to/right at the moment of starting
Closer to the moment than “とき” (immediacy)
Extends over a period of time, not a point
<ruby>授業<rt>じゅぎょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>けているあいだ
<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったら、<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して
Clearly indicates an absolute temporal relationship
<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>する<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に/<ruby>後<rt>ご</rt></ruby>で
